The Maestro · Part 5 · Phase 1 · 🏗️ Infrastructure hat

Site, Power and Cooling

Gopala does not own a building, a substation or a chiller. He rents a cluster inside someone else's data hall. So why does he need to understand power and cooling? Because they decide which halls can take his cluster at all, how dense his racks can be, how often a node throttles in summer, and a sizeable line in every price he pays. This part sizes Maestro-1's physical footprint from first principles with a small script, explains what changes between air- and liquid-cooled halls, and gives the site-visit checklist a renting start-up should use before the cluster is delivered.

1. Mission log: weeks 13–16

Week 13 · Sizing
  • Writes power_size.py (section 3) so he can check providers' answers about power density before signing (Part 4).
Week 15 · Site visit
  • Visits the chosen provider's data hall with the checklist below. Photographs the power path and the cooling plant; meets the on-site team that will swap his failed nodes.
Week 16 · Agreements
  • Agrees the rack layout, power feeds and maintenance windows in writing (maintenance windows), so a planned generator test cannot surprise his main run.

2. Why a renter needs facilities knowledge

  • A 1,024-GPU cluster is small by frontier standards (Meta trained Llama 3 405B on 16,384 H100s), but it is a large customer for most data halls: well over a megawatt in a few dozen racks.

The facility affects him in four ways:

  • Can it fit? Many existing halls were built for 5–15 kW racks. An 8-GPU H100 node alone can draw up to 10.2 kW.
  • Will it throttle? GPUs reduce their clocks when they run hot. A hall that cools well in spring but not at the August peak quietly slows the whole synchronised job, because the slowest GPU sets the pace.
  • Will it stop? A power event that drops a single rack can stop a job using every node. The power path (feeds, UPS, generators) sets how often that happens.
  • What does it cost? Power is passed through in GPU prices or billed directly; a less efficient hall costs more per useful hour.
  • For the full story of power and cooling at frontier scale, see the site's AI Compute Stack series on power and cooling and water
    • this part stays at Gopala's scale.

3. Sizing Maestro-1 from first principles

Maestro-1 in numbers

1.46 MWdesign IT load
1.17 MWtypical draw
333 tonscooling to remove
55%of node power is the GPUs

Real output of power_size.py (sustained draw and overheads are our assumptions).

Racks needed for 128 nodes, by rack power limit

15 kW racks (legacy)128 racks
40 kW racks (air, AI-ready)43 racks
130 kW racks (liquid)11 racks

Real output of power_size.py.

  • Four numbers decide the footprint: power per node, how much of that it really draws while training, the extra for networking and storage, and the facility overhead (PUE: total facility power divided by IT power).
power_size.py · Python 3, no dependencies
"""power_size.py — how much power, cooling and space Maestro-1 needs.

Gopala rents rather than builds, but he still has to know these numbers:
they decide which data halls can take his cluster at all, and they are
a line on every invoice that passes through power.
"""
NODES = 128                 # 1,024 GPUs, 8 per node
NODE_MAX_KW = 10.2          # DGX H100 maximum system power (NVIDIA user guide)
NODE_TYPICAL = 0.80         # our assumption: sustained draw ~80% of max in training
NET_STORAGE_KW = 0.12       # our assumption: switches, storage, management = +12% of IT
PUE = {"modern liquid-assisted hall": 1.25, "2025 global average": 1.54}
PRICE_KWH = 0.08            # our assumption, $ per kWh
RACK_LIMITS_KW = [15, 40, 130]   # legacy, air-cooled AI-ready, liquid (GB200 NVL72 class)

def main():
    it_max = NODES * NODE_MAX_KW * (1 + NET_STORAGE_KW)
    it_avg = NODES * NODE_MAX_KW * NODE_TYPICAL * (1 + NET_STORAGE_KW)
    print(f"IT load: {it_max/1000:.2f} MW design (max), {it_avg/1000:.2f} MW typical")
    for name, pue in PUE.items():
        fac = it_avg * pue
        mwh = fac * 730 / 1000
        print(f"  {name:28s} PUE {pue:.2f}: facility {fac/1000:.2f} MW, "
              f"{mwh:,.0f} MWh/month, ${mwh*1000*PRICE_KWH/1e3:,.0f}k/month")
    print("racks needed:")
    for lim in RACK_LIMITS_KW:
        per = int(lim // NODE_MAX_KW)
        if per == 0:
            print(f"  {lim:3d} kW racks: cannot hold one node"); continue
        racks = -(-NODES // per)
        print(f"  {lim:3d} kW racks: {per} nodes/rack -> {racks} racks")
    heat_btu = it_avg * 3412
    print(f"heat to remove: {it_avg:,.0f} kW = {heat_btu/12000:,.0f} tons of cooling")
    gpu_kw = NODES * 8 * 0.7
    print(f"GPUs alone at 700 W TDP: {gpu_kw:.0f} kW "
          f"({gpu_kw/(NODES*NODE_MAX_KW):.0%} of node max)")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
$ python3 power_size.py IT load: 1.46 MW design (max), 1.17 MW typical modern liquid-assisted hall PUE 1.25: facility 1.46 MW, 1,067 MWh/month, $85k/month 2025 global average PUE 1.54: facility 1.80 MW, 1,315 MWh/month, $105k/month racks needed: 15 kW racks: 1 nodes/rack -> 128 racks 40 kW racks: 3 nodes/rack -> 43 racks 130 kW racks: 12 nodes/rack -> 11 racks heat to remove: 1,170 kW = 333 tons of cooling GPUs alone at 700 W TDP: 717 kW (55% of node max)

What the numbers tell him:

  • About 1.5 MW of IT capacity must be reserved even though the typical draw is closer to 1.2 MW: the facility has to be built for the peak, and a training job hits near-peak during dense phases.
  • Rack density decides the room. In a legacy 15 kW hall, the cluster spreads over 128 racks, which means long cables between nodes and more switch layers. At 40 kW (a typical air-cooled AI-ready hall) it needs 43 racks; in a liquid-cooled hall, 11.
  • Efficiency is real money. The gap between a modern hall and the global average is about $20k a month at our assumed $0.08/kWh: ~$240k a year, enough to pay an engineer.
  • GPUs are only about half of a node's maximum power. CPUs, memory, NICs, NVSwitches, fans and power-conversion losses take the rest. Quoting "700 W × 1,024" under-sizes by half.

5. Air, liquid, or both

Cooling options by rack density

🌬️ Airup to ~30–40 kW per rack with containment
🚪 Rear-door heat exchanger~40–70 kW per rack
💧 Direct-to-chip liquid100+ kW per rack; needed for rack-scale systems

Industry ranges, not vendor specifications.

Every watt that goes in comes out as heat. There are three common ways to remove it from an AI rack:

ApproachTypical rackHow it worksFor Maestro-1
Airup to ~30–40 kW with hot/cold aisle containmentFans push air through servers; room units (CRAH) cool the air with chilled waterWorks for air-cooled H100 nodes at 3–4 per rack
Rear-door heat exchangers~40–70 kWA water-cooled coil on the back of each rack takes the heat out of exhaust airA common retrofit; denser racks in an old hall
Direct-to-chip liquid100+ kWCold plates on GPUs and CPUs, fed by a coolant distribution unit (CDU)Required by GB200 NVL72-class racks; optional for H100
  • H100 HGX nodes are sold in both air-cooled and liquid-cooled versions.
    • Gopala's provider offers air-cooled nodes in contained 40 kW racks, which is fine.
    • If his plan later moves to Blackwell-generation rack-scale systems, liquid cooling is not optional, and only some halls have it.
    • He writes that into the renewal options of the contract.
The throttling check
  • He asks for the hall's supply-air temperature history for last summer, and then watches GPU temperature and clock speed in his own telemetry (Part 7).
    • A node that is 5–10 °C hotter than its neighbours under the same load is usually a rack airflow problem, not a GPU problem, and is cheap to fix if found early.

6. The power path, and where it fails

The power path to one GPU

🏭UtilityGrid feed
⚡SubstationHigh → medium voltage
🔀SwitchgearTransformers, distribution
🔋UPSBatteries until generators start
🔌3 rack feedsEach feeds 2 of 6 node PSUs
🖥️NodeNeeds 4 of 6 PSUs powered

Every link has its own redundancy design; the last two are the ones a renter can check.

  • Electricity reaches a GPU through a chain: utility feed → substation → medium-voltage switchgear → transformers → UPS (batteries that bridge until generators start) → power distribution units → rack power strips → the node's power supplies.

Each link has a redundancy design:

  • N: no spare. One failure stops the load.
  • N+1: one spare unit for a group.
  • 2N: two fully independent paths (A and B feeds), each able to carry the whole load. Common in enterprise halls, and, as the cabling check below shows, not enough on its own for a 6-PSU H100 node.
  • The node has its own redundancy too.
    • NVIDIA's DGX H100 has six 3.3 kW power supplies in a 4+2 arrangement, and NVIDIA's design guide notes that at least four must be powered for the server to run.
    • That is why the same guide asks for three independent power sources per rack, each feeding two of the six supplies, so any one source can fail and four remain.
    • Gopala checks the arithmetic with a script below and asks to see the cabling, rack by rack.
  • AI training halls sometimes choose less redundancy than enterprise halls (for example, no UPS on some cooling loads), trading a small risk of a stop for lower cost, because a training job can restart from a checkpoint while a bank cannot.
    • That trade-off is acceptable for him only if his checkpoint strategy (Part 7) makes a stop cost minutes, not days.

7. Checking the power cabling with a script

Does a node survive losing one feed?

2 feeds: wirings that survive0 of 64
3 feeds: wirings that survive90 of 729
3 feeds, cabled 2+2+2always survives

Real output of psu_feeds.py.

  • Here the research changed Gopala's plan.
    • His first checklist (and the first version of this article) asked for the usual enterprise A/B feeds.
    • NVIDIA's SuperPOD design guide for H100 says something stricter: because four of the six power supplies must be energised, each rack needs three independent power sources, each connected to two of every node's six supplies, each from a separate upstream PDU, and each sized to carry half of the rack's expected peak.

The script checks why:

psu_feeds.py · Python 3, no dependencies
"""psu_feeds.py — does a node survive losing one power feed?

A DGX H100 has six power supplies and needs at least four energised.
NVIDIA's SuperPOD design guide therefore asks for THREE independent
sources per rack, each feeding two of the six supplies. This checks
every possible wiring with two and with three feeds.
"""
from itertools import product

NEED = 4

def survives(wiring, lost):
    return sum(1 for f in wiring if f != lost) >= NEED

def ok_all(w, feeds):
    return all(survives(w, f) for f in feeds)

def main():
    for feeds in ("AB", "ABC"):
        ways = list(product(feeds, repeat=6))
        good = [w for w in ways if ok_all(w, feeds)]
        print(f"{len(feeds)} feeds: {len(good)} of {len(ways)} wirings survive any one feed failing")
    cases = {"A/B, 3+3 (enterprise habit)": ("AAABBB", "AB"),
             "A/B/C, 2+2+2 (NVIDIA design)": ("AABBCC", "ABC"),
             "A/B/C, one cord on wrong strip": ("AAABCC", "ABC"),
             "A/B/C, C strip never cabled": ("AAABBB", "ABC")}
    for name, (w, feeds) in cases.items():
        res = "  ".join(f"lose {f}: {'runs' if survives(w, f) else 'STOPS'}" for f in feeds)
        print(f"  {name:32s} {res}")
    print("lesson: with a 4-of-6 minimum, two feeds can never protect the node;")
    print("        three feeds work only if every node is cabled 2+2+2 - check it rack by rack")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
$ python3 psu_feeds.py 2 feeds: 0 of 64 wirings survive any one feed failing 3 feeds: 90 of 729 wirings survive any one feed failing A/B, 3+3 (enterprise habit) lose A: STOPS lose B: STOPS A/B/C, 2+2+2 (NVIDIA design) lose A: runs lose B: runs lose C: runs A/B/C, one cord on wrong strip lose A: STOPS lose B: runs lose C: runs A/B/C, C strip never cabled lose A: STOPS lose B: STOPS lose C: runs lesson: with a 4-of-6 minimum, two feeds can never protect the node; three feeds work only if every node is cabled 2+2+2 - check it rack by rack
  • With two feeds, no wiring protects the node: one feed always ends up with three or fewer supplies.
    • With three, only the balanced 2+2+2 pattern (and its relabellings) survives the loss of any feed, and a single cord on the wrong strip quietly removes that protection.
    • So the site visit includes walking a sample of racks and reading power strip labels, and the provider's power monitoring is asked to show per-outlet current, which reveals a mis-cabled supply as a strip carrying more than its share.
Why this matters for a renter
  • A data hall built for 2N enterprise loads can host H100 nodes, but only if the rack power design follows the three-feed pattern.
    • It is a cheap thing to check before delivery and an expensive thing to discover during the main run, when a routine UPS maintenance on one feed would stop every node in the hall at once.

8. How cold is cold enough?

Two industry frameworks set the vocabulary for cooling conversations:

  • Air: ASHRAE's thermal guidelines define recommended and allowable ranges for server inlet air. Halls run inside the recommended envelope for reliability and use the wider allowable envelope only for short periods. Gopala asks for the hall's design inlet temperature and last summer's worst week, rather than for a single number.
  • Liquid: ASHRAE classifies liquid-cooled environments by the maximum temperature of the facility water supplied to the equipment. The fifth edition (2021) renamed the classes by that upper limit: W17, W27, W32, W40 (new), W45 and W+ (⚠️ via trade-press summaries). Warmer water means the facility can reject heat with dry coolers instead of chillers for more of the year, which lowers PUE and water use, but the equipment must be rated for it.
  • For Maestro-1 on air-cooled H100s, the practical check is simpler: inside his own telemetry (Part 7), GPU temperatures under full load should be consistent across racks, and no GPU should report thermal slowdown.
    • A rack row that runs several degrees hotter than the others is a facilities ticket, not a GPU ticket.

9. Training is a strange electrical load

  • A synchronised training job is not a steady load.
    • Thousands of GPUs compute together, then wait together for communication, then compute again, so power can swing quickly by a large fraction across the whole cluster.
    • Meta reported that power consumption across its Llama 3 training cluster fluctuated by tens of megawatts in step with the job, which stretches the limits of the power grid.
    • At 1.5 MW Gopala will not trouble a grid, but the swings still matter to the provider's UPS and generators.

Two practical consequences:

  • Tell the provider when a large job starts and stops; some ask for it.
  • Do not restart all 1,024 GPUs at the same second after a failure if the provider asks for a ramp. Part 7's restart logic can stagger it.

10. The site-visit checklist

A renter cannot design the building, but he can check it. Gopala's checklist, used on the scenario visit:

AreaQuestionGood answer
PowerRack power limit, and is it contracted per rack?≥ 40 kW per rack for air-cooled H100, written into the order
PowerHow many independent feeds per rack, and how are the six node PSUs split?Three feeds from separate upstream PDUs, each node cabled 2+2+2 (the cabling check)
PowerUPS runtime and generator test scheduleMinutes of UPS, monthly generator tests announced in advance
CoolingSupply temperature and the worst week last summerWithin ASHRAE's recommended range all year
CoolingContainment, and blanking panels in empty slotsHot or cold aisle contained; no gaps
SpaceAre all 128 nodes in one hall, close to the spine switches?Yes, with cable lengths that allow the planned fabric
PeopleWho swaps a node at 3 a.m., and where are spares?Staff on site 24/7, spare nodes and GPUs in the building
SecurityWho can enter the cage; how are failed drives handled?Named access list, drives destroyed on site with a record
WaterHow the hall uses water for coolingA stated water-use figure (WUE) and source
Scenario
  • On the visit, the hall meets every item except one: generator tests are monthly but not announced to tenants.
    • Gopala gets a clause requiring 7 days'
      • notice and agrees with the provider that tests will not be scheduled during the main run (maintenance windows).
    • The hall itself is not a real site.

11. Maintenance windows and change freezes

  • Facilities have to be maintained: UPS batteries replaced, generators tested, switchgear inspected.
    • Each event carries a small risk of a stop.

The agreement Gopala signs:

  • A 30-day change freeze on his racks' power and cooling during the main run (months 9–10.5), except for emergencies.
  • 7 days' notice for any planned work that touches his power path.
  • A shared calendar so the provider's maintenance and his checkpoints line up: take a checkpoint before planned work, not after.

12. If the next model needs liquid cooling

  • Rack-scale systems such as NVIDIA's GB200 NVL72 put 72 GPUs in one liquid-cooled rack drawing on the order of 120 kW or more (⚠️ exact figures vary by configuration), roughly ten times what the hall above was built for per rack.
    • If Maestro-2 is trained on such systems, the facility question changes from "does the hall have enough space?"
      • to "does the hall have facility water at the rack, coolant distribution units and a floor that can take the weight?".
    • Only a subset of halls do, and they are booked early.
    • That is why Part 4's contract includes an upgrade path, and why Gopala keeps a short list of providers with liquid-cooled capacity even though he does not need it yet.
    • The site's cooling and water article covers the engineering.

13. Facility data a renter should ask for

SignalWhere it comes fromWhat he uses it for
Per-outlet power on rack PDUsIntelligent rack PDUsSpotting mis-cabled supplies; real power per node
Rack inlet temperatureSensors at the cold aisleSeparating airflow problems from GPU problems
Planned maintenance calendarFacilities teamTaking a checkpoint before work on a feed
Incident reportsFacilities teamMatching a job failure to a power or cooling event
Monthly energy and PUEBuilding management systemCost and emissions reporting
  • Most providers can export some of this through an API or a portal.
    • Getting it into the same dashboards as GPU metrics (Part 7) is what lets him answer the question "was that us or the building?" in minutes.

14. Five facility mistakes renters make

  1. Sizing to GPU TDP (700 W × GPUs) instead of node maximum power, and running out of rack power.
  2. Accepting 2N A/B feeds for 6-PSU nodes without checking the cabling (the cabling check).
  3. Splitting the cluster across halls to fit low-density racks, then paying in cable lengths and extra switch layers.
  4. Never asking about maintenance windows until a generator test lands in the middle of a run.
  5. Treating hot nodes as bad GPUs and replacing hardware that was fine.

15. The environmental footprint

  • Investors and design partners now ask.
    • From the script: about 1,070–1,320 MWh a month while the cluster runs hard, depending on the hall's efficiency.
    • Emissions depend entirely on the local grid mix, which differs by more than ten times between regions, so Gopala asks the provider for the grid's carbon intensity and any renewable contracts that cover the hall, and reports the number in his model card later (Part 14) rather than making a claim he cannot back.

18. The series

The Maestro: 18 parts in five phases

Verdict
  • Renting the building does not remove the physics: Maestro-1 needs about 1.5 MW of IT capacity, dense racks, a power path that will not stop the job, and a change freeze during the main run.
    • Next, Part 6: the cluster arrives, and nothing is trusted until it is tested.

19. Reading the numbers

Primary / standard
DGX H100: 6 × 3.3 kW PSUs, 4+2 redundancy, 10.2 kW maximum (NVIDIA user guide); four of six must be energised, three power sources per rack each feeding two PSUs, each path sized for half the rack's peak (NVIDIA SuperPOD H100 data-centre design guide). H100 700 W TDP. Llama 3 trained on 16,384 H100s; power swings across the cluster (Meta).
Secondary ⚠️
ASHRAE liquid-cooling classes W17–W45 and W+ (5th edition naming, via trade press). Global average PUE ~1.54 in 2025 (Uptime Institute survey, as reported by secondary coverage); 1.52 capacity-weighted in Uptime's 2026 survey. Typical rack densities by cooling type are industry ranges.
Our assumptions
Sustained draw at 80% of maximum, +12% for network and storage, PUE 1.25 for a modern hall, $0.08/kWh, the site visit and agreements.
